name: Web Application Hunt
author: AppSec Hunt Team
prerequisites: Web server access logs available for the hunt window
Read access to web root directories on target servers
required_tools: GoAccess or AWStats for log analysis
ClamAV or YARA for webshell scanning
grep / awk / jq for log parsing

hunt_actions.title: Webshell Detection
actions: Scan web root directories for known webshell signatures using YARA: `yara -r /path/to/webshell_rules.yar /var/www/html/ 2>/dev/null` — use Neo23x0's webshell YARA ruleset (https://github.com/Neo23x0/signature-base). Also: `find /var/www -name '*.php' -newer /var/www/index.php -ls 2>/dev/null | sort -k8` for recently modified PHP files.

Detect webshell execution patterns in access logs: `grep -E '(cmd|exec|shell|passthru|eval|base64_decode|system|phpinfo|assert)' /var/log/nginx/access.log | grep -v '404\|301\|302' | awk '{print $1, $7, $9}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20` — encoded POST body parameters are harder to detect; also check for abnormally large POST requests to static file extensions (.jpg, .png, .pdf).

Hunt for one-line PHP webshells using ClamAV: `clamscan -r --infected --no-summary /var/www/html/ 2>/dev/null | grep -v ': OK'` — ensure ClamAV database is freshly updated with `freshclam` before scanning. Flag any PHP file under 5KB in an upload directory.

Identify base64-encoded payloads in web requests: `grep -a 'base64' /var/log/nginx/access.log | awk '{print $1, $6, $7}' | grep 'POST\|PUT' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -30` — also decode suspicious values: `echo '<base64_string>' | base64 -d` to inspect payload content.

hunt_actions.title: Exploitation Attempt Detection
actions: Hunt for SQL injection attempts in web logs: `grep -E "('|--|;|UNION|SELECT|INSERT|DROP|xp_cmdshell|EXEC|CAST|CONVERT|CHAR|NCHAR|VARCHAR|WAITFOR)" /var/log/apache2/access.log | grep -v '404' | awk '{print $1, $7, $9}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20` — URL-decode the URI before analysis: `python3 -c "import sys,urllib.parse; [print(urllib.parse.unquote(l)) for l in sys.stdin]"`

Detect directory traversal and LFI/RFI attempts: `grep -E '(\.\./|%2e%2e%2f|%252e%252e%252f|/etc/passwd|/proc/self|php://|expect://)' /var/log/nginx/access.log | awk '{print $1, $6, $7, $9}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20`

Identify server-side template injection (SSTI) attempts: `grep -E '(\{\{|\{%|\$\{|#\{|<%|\[\[)' /var/log/apache2/access.log | grep -vE '404|301|302|\.(js|css|ico)' | awk '{print $1, $6, $7}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`

Review WAF block and pass-through logs: In your WAF portal (e.g., ModSecurity, AWS WAF, Cloudflare), filter for RuleId matches within the OWASP Core Rule Set (CRS). Specifically check for rules 930100-930130 (LFI), 931100-931130 (RFI), 941100-941999 (XSS), 942100-942999 (SQLi) that were ALLOWED (not blocked) — these represent bypass attempts that succeeded past the WAF.

hunt_actions.title: Post-Exploitation Web Activity
actions: Detect unusual outbound connections from the web server: `ss -tnp | grep -E ':(80|443|8080|8443)' | awk '{print $5}'` for live connections, and `netstat -antp 2>/dev/null | grep ESTABLISHED | grep -v ':80\|:443' | grep httpd\|nginx\|apache` — web server processes should not be initiating outbound connections.

Hunt for command execution output in HTTP responses: `grep -E 'HTTP/1\.[01]" (200|201|204)' /var/log/nginx/access.log | awk '{print $7, $10}' | sort -k2 -rn | head -30` — unusually large response sizes (> 10,000 bytes) to POST requests on static pages indicate data retrieval via webshell.

Identify cron jobs or new files created by web server user: `find / -user www-data -o -user apache -o -user nginx -type f -newer /var/log/dpkg.log -ls 2>/dev/null | grep -v '/proc\|/sys\|/var/log'` — and `crontab -u www-data -l 2>/dev/null` — the web server user should not own any files outside the web root or have any scheduled tasks.

questions: Are web server access logs (Apache/Nginx) retained for the full hunt window, and do they include the full request URI, response code, response size, and X-Forwarded-For header if behind a load balancer?
Is a Web Application Firewall (WAF) deployed in front of all public-facing applications, and are WAF logs (including both blocked and allowed request decisions) forwarded to the SIEM?
Is there a current, complete inventory of all web applications and services exposed on the network perimeter, including version information and responsible application owners?

Are web application dependencies (frameworks, libraries, CMS plugins) tracked in a software bill of materials (SBOM), and are vulnerable versions identified via automated scanning (e.g., OWASP Dependency-Check)?
Are upload directories and writable web root paths isolated and restricted from server-side script execution (e.g., php_flag engine off in .htaccess, or location block in Nginx config)?
Is file integrity monitoring (FIM) configured specifically on the web root directories to detect unauthorized file creation or modification in real time or near-real time?
Are web server processes running under a dedicated, least-privilege service account with no interactive login shell, no sudo rights, and restricted filesystem write permissions?
Are error logs (PHP error_log, application stack traces) suppressed from HTTP responses in the production environment to prevent information disclosure to potential attackers?
